ac:layout-cell.p: We want the BFI customer app (bravo-customer-app) to follow the DK Jago app (digital_banking_app). This page compares the two. It lists the gaps and suggests an order of work.

li.p: CI/CD and basic security are closer to Jago than expected. BFI already obfuscates release builds and pins certificates. It checks for rooted devices, uses Play Integrity and App Attest, uploads to Play and TestFlight, and has a manual approval gate for prod.

Architecture is the biggest gap. BFI has no domain layer and no module boundaries. Screens and controllers use API models (DTOs) directly. Jago has a pure-Dart domain layer, feature modules, and written layer rules.

Analytics needs one wrapper. BFI sends events two ways: 187 Firebase logEvent calls with 148 hard-coded event names, mostly in screens, and a separate typed Mixpanel tracker. Jago has one analytics interface that fans out to every platform, with typed events. This is the best quick win.

Testing has no safety net. BFI's PR pipeline rejects controller tests. No coverage threshold is enforced. There are no end-to-end tests. Jago gates coverage on changed files and runs Appium end-to-end tests.

App protection is missing. Jago wraps every prod build with Everspin (anti-tamper and code protection) and registers each build. BFI has nothing like this, and Android code shrinking (R8) is on, but not set explicitly. Corrected 14 Oct 2026 after team review: R8 is on through Flutter's default; an earlier version said it was probably off.
One urgent security item: a GitHub workflow in the repo is built to print prod secrets in readable form. See the Security items section below.
No second app. Features stay identical through one loop: old and new path behind a switch flag, same tests on both, slow rollout, then delete the old path. See Keeping features identical below.

td.p: Repo layout
Melos workspace. 4 apps, 49 module_* packages (features + shared), 110 library/* wrappers around pub.dev packages.
Melos workspace with 3 packages: digital (the app, 23 features), data/customer (API + models), shared_lib/core.
Every feature lives in one package. Nothing stops one feature from importing another.
L
Layering

data → domain ← presentation in every feature. Domain is pure Dart. Features talk through thin *_api contract packages. Rules are written down in .claude/rules/layer-model.md and journey-clean-architecture.md.
Screen → controller (StateNotifier) → sometimes a use case → repository → HttpClient. No domain/ folder anywhere. Repositories return API models straight to the UI.
API changes reach the screens directly. Business rules sit in controllers and screens.
L
State management
bloc, with rules: no BuildContext or navigation inside blocs.
Riverpod 2.6 with the old StateNotifier API. 72 controllers. A global appRef is used in 142 places.
Keep Riverpod. Move to Notifier / AsyncNotifier. Remove the global appRef.
M
Dependency injection
injectable + get_it. Each module exposes a micro-package. Wiring happens only in the app layer.
Riverpod providers (128 static final provider). Environment objects are injected with ProviderScope.overrides in main.dart.
Riverpod is fine as DI. The gap is module boundaries: each feature package should expose its providers, and the app should wire them.
M (comes with layering)
Analytics wrapper

AnalyticsPlatform interface. One fan-out sends each event to Datadog, Firebase and CleverTap. Events are typed classes (AnalyticsEventV2), with name constants in about 55 files. Widgets fire an event; a bloc dispatches it.

Two separate paths. Firebase: 187 logEvent calls in 81 files, 148 event names as plain strings, almost all in screens. Mixpanel: a typed EventTracker, plus automatic tracking in the Digital* components. AppsFlyer and Insider have their own services.
No single interface. No event catalogue. Adding or replacing a platform means touching 80+ files.
S–M
Logging and crashes
Monitoring fans out to Crashlytics and Datadog. PII is cleaned by jago_observability_sanitizer.dart.
DatadogLog (59 mentions in app code; corrected 9 Oct: the earlier "90 uses" counted test files) forwards errors to Crashlytics with trace and session IDs. Flutter and platform errors are caught.
Good. Add a PII cleaner before logs leave the device.
S
Feature flags
Typed flag catalogue (BoolFeatureFlag, IntFeatureFlag, …) behind one FeatureFlagPlatform interface. Providers: Firebase Remote Config, Split.io, GrowthBook.
One very wide RemoteConfig model (its generated file is 2,443 lines), plus Mixpanel flags for experiments.
No typed catalogue, and no single interface across Remote Config and Mixpanel.
M
Networking
dio adapter behind a client interface. 17 typed exception classes mapped to error messages. Not interceptor-based yet (their own TODO).
One dio wrapper (http_client.dart, 496 lines). Token refresh and the 401 retry live inside the client, not in an interceptor. Errors are mapped to typed exceptions with x-trace-id.
Move auth, refresh and retry into dio interceptors. Split the client by concern.
S
Security

Everspin Eversafe anti-tamper (Android and iOS), CodeMix code protection on every prod build, each build registered for forgery checks, TrustDecision device fingerprint, screen-capture guard, certificate pinning.

Certificate pinning, root/jailbreak check (behind a flag), Play Integrity / App Attest (x-integrity-id header), Dart --obfuscate. No minifyEnabled on the Android release build, so R8 is probably not running. API_SECRET is built into the app.
No anti-tamper (RASP) or code protection. R8 likely off.
S (R8) / M (RASP, needs vendor)
Design system
module_design_library: tokens generated from a Figma export, brand and theme switching, Widgetbook published to GitLab Pages.

In-app Digital* classes (32, across app/ui, app/widget and app/theme) and theme in digital/lib/app/. Used well: 250 lines use DigitalButton vs 0 raw Material buttons, 1,040 lines use DigitalColors vs 49 raw colours. Corrected 9 Oct: earlier counts (16 / 454 / 795 / 39) were wrong; the conclusion is the same.
No separate package. No token pipeline from Figma. No Widgetbook.
M
Testing
About 5,288 test files. Coverage gate on changed files per module. End-to-end tests with Appium + Cucumber on BrowserStack.

193 test files, 1,039 widget tests, mostly whole screens. The PR pipeline rejects *_controller_test.dart files. Coverage is uploaded to Codacy and Sonar. Corrected 9 Oct: master requires a "Codacy Diff Coverage" check, so a threshold may exist in Codacy settings (not visible in the repo). No integration or end-to-end tests in this repo; a separate mobile suite exists in automation-monorepo (WebdriverIO + Appium, 15 specs, no register or KYC spec).
Logic can't be tested on its own. Unclear whether anything blocks a coverage drop. Nothing tests full journeys.
M
Lint and guardrails
custom_lint rules, Danger bot, checks for generated files and package use, .claude/rules (14 files) and skills, including an mr-review skill.
lint/strict, dart format check and flutter analyze via melos run analyze, generated-code check on merge, AGENTS.md.
No architecture checks. No review bot.
S
CI/CD
See the next section.
GitHub Actions, 13 workflows.
See the next section.

ac:layout-cell.h3: 1. A workflow can print prod secrets in readable form (urgent)

li.p: File:.github/workflows/test.yaml, named "Reveal Secret".
Added: commit 70ed19f3, 31 Dec 2025. It is still on master, and (added 9 Oct) also on all four release branches release-2.24.x to release-2.27.x. The GitHub API shows no pull request for that commit.

What it does: it runs on manual dispatch, inside the customer_app_prod environment. It echoes three secrets: BRAVO_GCP_SA_KEY, KNOWN_HOSTS and SSH_PRIVATE_KEY. Each one is piped through sed 's/./& /g', which puts a space between every character.

Why that matters: GitHub hides a secret in logs only when the exact value appears. With spaces added, the value no longer matches, so the full GCP service-account key and SSH private key would show in the job log. Anyone who can read the run logs could read them.

History: the workflow has run once, on 31 Dec 2025. That run failed before any step started (the job shows no steps), so the secrets were most likely not printed. This was checked through the GitHub API; the log itself was not opened.
Delete test.yaml from master and every release branch.
Rotate BRAVO_GCP_SA_KEY and SSH_PRIVATE_KEY anyway. They were exposed to anyone who could run the workflow, and that is the safe default.
Add required reviewers to the customer_app_prod environment (added 9 Oct: today none of the 6 environments has any protection rule), so no workflow can use prod secrets without approval.
Add a CI check that fails any workflow which echoes secrets.*.

Prod builds without approval (added 9 Oct). build-prod-artifact.yml builds a prod-signed APK and IPA inside customer_app_prod with no approval. The approval in build-prod.yml is a job step, not an environment rule. PRs that only change .github/** skip CI.

Personal data in analytics (added 9 Oct). The apply_loan event sends the full home address (customer_address) to Firebase (home_loan_simulation.dart:368). Loan amount, monthly income, marital status and loan purpose go to Mixpanel. Datadog tracking consent is hard-coded to granted (main.dart:42). Handled first in Mobile plan 02.
Root check default (added 9 Oct). The check is on in prod through a GitHub variable, but the code default is off. If the variable goes missing, the check silently stops.

R8: on, but implicit. Corrected 14 Oct 2026 after team review: R8 is on through Flutter's default; an earlier version said it was probably off. The Flutter Gradle plugin enables R8 whenever its shrink property is not false, and nothing in BFI sets it. Production crashes in Datadog carry r8-map-id frames with readable names, so the mapping.txt upload works too. What remains: set minifyEnabled explicitly so a tooling change cannot switch it off silently, fail the prod build if mapping.txt is missing, and review the keep rules against every SDK.
API_SECRET is built into the app and sent on every request. Treat it as public, because anyone can pull it out of the app. Do not let the backend rely on it for security.
project.pbxproj is tracked even though .gitignore excludes it. A project.pbxproj.backup copy is also tracked. Decide which one is the source of truth and delete the backup.
No anti-tamper (RASP). Jago uses Everspin Eversafe. For a lending app that handles KYC, this is worth a vendor decision.

td.p: Security

A workflow on master and 4 release branches can print prod secrets. No GitHub environment has a protection rule. R8 already runs through Flutter's default, but it is not set explicitly and its keep rules were never reviewed. Nothing stops screenshots of KYC or PIN screens.

Prod secrets cannot be printed or used without an approver. R8 is set explicitly with reviewed keep rules, so a tooling change cannot switch it off silently. Sensitive screens are blank in screenshots. The backend stops trusting a secret anyone can pull out of the APK.
Removes a live key-leak path and an audit finding waiting to happen. Fewer fraud and account-takeover cases from tampered apps once RASP is in.
Audit, fraud, every user
Analytics wrapper

187 Firebase calls in 81 files with 148 event names typed as strings. A second, separate Mixpanel path. The customer's full home address goes to Firebase; income and loan amount go to Mixpanel. Datadog consent is hard-coded to granted.
One interface, typed events, one catalogue. Personal data is blocked before it leaves the device. Consent is real. Dashboards keep the same event names.

Closes a personal-data exposure to two third parties. New events take minutes, not a hunt through 80 files. Swapping or adding a vendor touches 1 file. Product analytics can review every event in one place.
Data protection, product analytics, marketing
Testing
Controller tests are rejected by CI. Logic can only be tested through whole screens. No coverage threshold we can see. No end-to-end run before a release.

Logic is tested on its own, fast. Coverage on changed files is a hard gate (start 70%). Register, KYC, loan submission and payment run on real devices for every release candidate. The parity net lets us refactor with proof.
Fewer regressions reach customers. PRs get faster, because unit tests replace slow screen tests. Every later plan can change code without guessing.
Squad, QA, release manager
CI/CD

README says Flutter 3.38.5, CI uses 3.41.9. Build numbers come from a tag. 13 workflows, 2,943 lines, 279 of them repeated --dart-define flags. One workflow builds prod-signed apps with no approval. Workflow-only PRs skip CI.

One Flutter version in one file. Build numbers always go up. Prod builds need an approver. Workflows under 1,500 lines. Staged rollout on Play with a crash check between stages. A monthly report on how fast and how safely we ship.
Fewer broken builds from version drift. Faster, safer releases. A bad release reaches 10% of users, not 100%. Delivery metrics we can show management.
Squad, SRE, management
Logging and crashes
35 of 38 Datadog error calls put raw error text in the message. No PII cleaner. Trace ID reaches Crashlytics but not Datadog logs, so support cannot jump from a crash to the backend trace.
One monitoring interface. A PII cleaner runs before anything leaves the device, proven by a unit test and a weekly zero-hit query. Every error carries the backend trace ID.
Support finds the cause of a customer problem in minutes instead of hours. Personal data stops landing in Datadog and Crashlytics. Crash rates can be split by old and new path during rollouts.
Support, SRE, data protection
Lint and guardrails
Rules exist only in AGENTS.md and reviewers' heads. 264 feature-to-feature imports today, and nothing stops the 265th.
A checker in CI fails any PR that adds new debt: feature-to-feature imports, Flutter in domain code, vendor SDKs outside adapters, overdue switch flags. The baseline only goes down.
The architecture work cannot be undone by the next sprint. Reviews are shorter, because the tool catches the mechanical part. AI tools and new joiners read the same written rules.
Squad, tech lead, new joiners
Networking
One 496-line HTTP client. Token refresh has a real race: several late 401s can each start a new refresh. No request ID on requests.
Small interceptors, each with one job. Single-flight refresh, proven by 7 race tests. Every request carries a request ID and keeps the server trace ID. The 114 repository call sites do not change.
Fewer random logouts and failed requests under load. Backend and mobile logs line up on one ID. A bug in auth or retry is found in a 40-line file, not a 500-line one.
Every user, support, backend team
Layering
No domain layer. 214 of 355 feature files import API models straight into screens and controllers. Business rules sit in 1,000-line screens and a 970-line KYC use case.
Every feature has data, domain and presentation. Rules live in pure Dart with their own unit tests. An API change stops at the data layer. loan first, then auth, rl, ro.
A backend field change no longer breaks screens. Rules like tenor, due dates and KYC skips are tested in milliseconds without a widget. New features in loan get faster to build and safer to change.
Squad, product, backend team
State management
72 controllers on the legacy StateNotifier API. A global appRef used in 142 places and a global navigatorContext in 151, so code can reach anything from anywhere.
Riverpod 3 Notifier everywhere. No globals. Notifiers hold state, call use cases, never navigate, and have unit tests.
Riverpod stays supported (the legacy API is on its way out). Bugs are reproducible in a unit test instead of only on a phone. Memory leaks from stale global reads go away.
Squad
Dependency injection
4 ports overridden inline in main.dart. 128 providers with no boundary; any feature can read any other.
Each feature declares its own providers and reads outside things only through ports. All wiring in one place. A CI test proves every port is wired.
A missing wiring is caught in CI, not at app start on a customer's phone. Tests swap real services for fakes in one line. Same mechanism carries the switch flags for safe rollouts.
Squad, QA
Repo layout
All 23 features in one package. 60 feature pairs import each other, 14 of them in both directions. router.dart (870 lines) imports every feature.
loan, auth, rl, ro are their own packages with a small public surface. A feature cannot import another by accident, because the package does not depend on it.
Two squads can work on two features without stepping on each other. Builds and tests can run per package. A feature can be reused in another BFI app later.
Squad leads, future apps
Feature flags
One 44-field Remote Config model (2,443 generated lines), read in 44 files. Mixpanel flags on a separate path. 2 flags nobody reads. No owner or removal date on any flag.
A typed catalogue: key, safe default, owner, removal date. One port over Remote Config and Mixpanel. CI fails when a flag is overdue. Switch flags for safe rollouts live here.
Flags stop piling up. A flag change rebuilds only the widgets that read it. Rollouts and kill switches become a routine, not a one-off.
Product, squad
32 Digital* components inside the app package, no Widgetbook, 49 raw colour literals. Adoption is already high, so this is the smallest gap.
Components and theme in their own package, every component visible in Widgetbook, colours and spacing as named tokens, optional Figma sync.
Designers and engineers check a component without running the app. UI drift between screens drops. Golden tests catch an unintended visual change.
Design, squad

li.p: Customers: fewer random logouts and failed requests (07), fewer regressions in each release (03, 04), a bad release stopped at 10% of users instead of 100% (04), and an app that is harder to tamper with (01).

Compliance and audit: the secret-leak path closed and prod builds behind an approver (01, 04), personal data blocked from analytics and logs with a weekly proof (02, 05), real consent (02), an OWASP MASVS table kept per quarter (01).
Support and SRE: one ID from a customer complaint to a crash to the backend trace (05, 07), readable Android stack traces after R8 (01), crash and error rates split by rollout group (04, 05).
Product: new events reviewed in one catalogue (02), flags with owners and removal dates (12), rollouts and kill switches as a routine (04, 12), delivery metrics every month (04).

Engineering: rules tested in milliseconds without a widget (08, 09), a CI checker that stops new debt (06), features in their own packages so squads do not collide (11), a Widgetbook for the UI kit (13).

ac:layout-cell.p: Plans 01 to 06 are small and pay back in the first one or two sprints each. Plans 07 to 11 are the architecture work; their benefit grows feature by feature, starting with loan. Plans 12 and 13 are useful but nothing else waits on them.

We do not build a second app. We improve the one BFI app in place. For each risky change, the old and the new code live side by side in the same app, behind a switch flag. The same tests run on both paths. Then we roll out slowly, compare the two groups of users, flip, and delete the old path. Each plan below applies this in its own Parity check block.

li.p: Users would have to move. A second app needs a new bundle id. Users reinstall, and their secure storage (tokens, PIN state) does not move. Or it replaces the current app in one big-bang cut-over.
Parity drifts from day one. The current app ships every week (Monday release branch). A parallel app has to chase every change for months.
Too big to rewrite safely. 23 features, 78 routes, 264 cross-feature imports.
Jago did not do it either. Its rule is a ratchet plus "extract and flip" inside one app. Its second app shell is for a second bank, not for parity.
Second apps we do want: internal ones only, never in the stores: Widgetbook for the design system, and a sandbox app per feature package.
Freeze. Write the parity ledger for the feature. Make sure the parity net passes on the old path.
Build beside. The new path is added next to the old one. The old code is not changed.
Switch flag. One Remote Config flag per feature (for example useNewLoanFlow), default = old path, with an owner and a removal date. QA also gets a dev-mode toggle.

Same tests, both paths. The parity net must pass with the flag off and on: golden screenshots, recorded SIT API fixtures, widget tests run twice, the analytics golden names file, and the e2e journeys in automation-monorepo.

Cohort check. Roll the flag out 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, with Play staged rollout. Compare old and new users in Datadog RUM (crash-free sessions, errors, load time) and in Firebase/Mixpanel funnels. If a threshold breaks, flip the flag back.
Flip and delete. After 2 releases at 100% with no regression, delete the old path and the flag. A feature has parity only when its old path is gone.

ac:layout-cell.p: Each phase is one Jira epic. Each step is one ticket. See Mobile roadmap: step by step.

li.p: Who owns this plan? The Customer Mobile Apps squad, with a named tech lead.

RASP vendor and budget. Start with the free layer now (R8, root check fail-safe, backend enforcing Play Integrity and App Attest verdicts). Then quotes and a proof of concept from Promon, Guardsquare, Appdome and V-Key, all scored on one PoC scorecard (add Everspin and DoveRunner if local Indonesian support is a must-have). Mind the licence model: per active user or per download grows with our customer base; a flat fee per app does not. Talsec freeRASP can be trialled in SIT, but its free tier is capped at 100,000 devices and sends telemetry to Talsec, so production needs the paid tier. Full options, including open-source ones, are in Mobile plan 01: Security, step 7.
Coverage threshold. What number for changed files? A suggested start is 70%, raised over time.

Separate prod pipeline repo? Jago keeps prod signing and distribution in a separate repo. That gives a smaller blast radius, but it is more to maintain. BFI could get most of the benefit by protecting the GitHub environment instead.

Design system: build our own, or adopt DK's library? Mobile plan 13 assumes BFI builds its own package. The "Mobile development with DK" session (Aug 2026) floated BFI adopting the Jago library and joining a shared design community. Trade-off: full control and our own look, versus faster start and a dependency on DK's roadmap. The comparison is in Mobile plan 14 (designer guide). Needs product and management, not only the squad.
